title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: generic both-subtree traversal versus exploiting BST ordering to discard one subtree per comparison.

content.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer val, find the node in the BST whose value equals val, and return the subtree rooted at that node. If no such node exists, return null.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Binary SEARCH tree\" explicitly named","The left subtree holds smaller values, the right subtree holds larger values, enabling a binary-search-like traversal"],["A single target value to locate","Compare val to the current node and go left or right accordingly, discarding the other half of the tree"]]}

blocks.text: In a BST, every node's left subtree contains only smaller values, and its right subtree only larger values. This means at any node, comparing val to that node's value immediately tells you which subtree (if any) could possibly contain val, letting you discard the other subtree entirely.

blocks.title: Analogy: Searching a Filing Cabinet Sorted by Number
blocks.text: Picture a filing cabinet where folders are arranged so anything to the left of a divider is numbered lower, and anything to the right is numbered higher, at every level of organization. Looking for a specific number, you only ever need to check one side at each level, never both.

blocks.caption: At each node, compare val to decide whether to search left, right, or stop

blocks.text: Result subtree (preorder): 2 1 null null 3 null null, the subtree rooted at the node with value 2.

Before checking every node with a generic traversal, notice the BST property means each comparison at a node eliminates an entire subtree from consideration, exactly like binary search on a sorted array.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If val equals the current node's value, that node (and its subtree) is the answer.

Observation 2: If val is less than the current node's value, the BST property guarantees it can only exist (if at all) in the LEFT subtree.

Observation 3: Symmetrically, if val is greater, only the RIGHT subtree needs checking.

Observation 4: Repeating this at each level discards half the remaining tree (on average, for a balanced tree) every step, giving O(height) time instead of O(n).
This leads to a loop (or simple recursion): compare val to the current node, move left or right accordingly, stopping when found or when reaching null.
Traverse every node of the tree (e.g., via any standard traversal), checking each for a match, ignoring the BST ordering entirely.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking both subtrees at every node correctly finds the target regardless of tree structure.
It completely ignores the BST ordering property, costing O(n) instead of O(height).

blocks.text: Limitation: the BST property lets each comparison discard an entire subtree, achieving O(height) instead of O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Since the left subtree only ever holds smaller values and the right only larger, comparing val to the current node directly determines which single subtree to descend into, never both.

This can be implemented iteratively (a simple loop) or recursively, following left or right based on the comparison until val is found or a null is reached.
Compare val to the current node; move left if smaller, right if larger, return the node if equal, or null if a leaf's child is reached without a match.

The BST invariant guarantees val can only exist in the direction the comparison points, so discarding the other subtree at every step never loses the target if it exists, while halving (on average) the remaining search space.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(height), O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) worst case for a skewed one.
Space: O(1) for the iterative version.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "binary SEARCH tree, find a value", think: compare and discard one subtree at each step, just like binary search.
